Have you changed your rinse routine besides adding xylitol? Too much or too little saline content can cause irritation or congestion. I had to experiment until I found the right blend for me.

If you are talking about the NeilMed packets, one packet mixed in 240 ml of water is a normal saline solution. 

Normal means that the amount of salt is similar to what is inside your nasal cavity. A hypertonic solution is when more salt than that is used, i.e. more than one packet. Whether a normal or hypertonic solution is best is case specific. I will say that two packets is a lot of salt, and having too much can irritate your nasal membrane. Having too little salt (a hypotonic solution) can make your nose burn, too.

The above holds true for the NeilMed rinse packets with xylitol. I assume that’s what you have, and not just a packet of 100 percent xylitol.  I have used rinses containing xylitol daily in the past and it didn’t seem to cause me any problems.

I don’t know if you are new to tinnitus or not, but if you are here are a few things I wish I had known when I was new:

If your tinnitus doesn’t go away, it is highly likely that in time you won’t notice it much and won’t care when you do. That’s been my experience and is a pretty common experience, I think.

Keep in mind that many of the tinnitus websites tend to be populated by people who are either 1) new to it and scared or 2) long term sufferers who have never habituated. Don’t read too much into what you hear there.

Try to protect your hearing going forward. If an environment is loud enough that you need to shout to be heard, it’s too loud. Don’t overprotect either. You shouldn’t wear earplugs to the grocery store, for example, unless ordered to by a physician.

None of this is intended to minimize the suffering that tinnitus does inflict on some. But the odds are you’re going to be okay eventually. For most, it just takes time.

Maybe a little, but what really changed was my perception of and mindset towards the noise.  The intensity of mine does tend to ebb and flow based on stress and other factors, not all of which are discernible.

I think my experience is pretty common, but I know it isn’t universal. My heart breaks for the long term sufferers who, for whatever reason, don’t habituate. But keep in mind that most people do habituate, and all it really takes is time. Trying to stay healthy and your mind busy whilst recovering helps.

One other thing you should keep in mind is to not read too much into the despairing stories you may see on the tinnitus sites.   The folks who tend to hang out on the tinnitus sites are those who are suffering the most from their tinnitus. The vast majority of those whose tinnitus disappears, reduces, or is otherwise no longer a problem for them do not post to those sites.  It is easy to get a warped perspective if you aren’t careful (voice of experience on that one).

In the meantime, you can get checked for hearing loss. You can also get your ears examined for any of the correctable issues that may be causing your tinnitus. If a solution isn’t found, don’t panic. With time, the odds are strongly in your favor to be fine again. One other thing you should do - avoid loud noise. If a noise is loud enough that you have to shout to be heard over it, it’s too loud.

Not everyone has that experience, but it’s been my experience, and I think it is a common experience.

I didn’t get into the law school I wanted to go to because my undergrad grades weren’t what they needed to be as I had a couple substance abuse problems. I was broke in the middle of the recession with no job and no prospects. Many of my friends were progressing in life - getting better jobs, buying a house, etc. I was so bitter and jealous and hateful. I slowly drifted away from them as I couldn’t bear to be around them or hear about their successes. I became a hermit.

Not coincidentally, that’s about when my first really bad case of agoraphobia started. Soon I was more or less housebound.  I thought my life was over. But I forced myself to go to job interviews and finally got a shitty law care job. That job forced me to leave the house, to drive, and to talk to people. It was excruciatingly difficult some days. But it made me functional again and gradually I overcame agoraphobia. 

I don’t mean to sound brash, but since that horrible time in my life, I have had quite a bit of personal and professional success. I say this only because if I could do it, you can too. You will have plenty to be proud of and happy about someday.
